newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-NO KIDDING, LIPINSKI IS WORLD CHAMPION.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-NO KIDDING, LIPINSKI IS WORLD CHAMPION.

text.p: Ten months after ice skating officials introduced a rule banning anyone under 15 from competing, a 14-year-old American was on Saturday crowned world champion.
Tara Lipinski, given special dispensation to enter because she took part last year, edged out her 16-year-old compatriot Michelle Kwan to become the youngest ever women's champion.
It was an occasion Lipinski had been working towards since as a six-year-old she practised climbing on top of a podium her father had built for her at their home.

The 1.47-metre, 35-kg sprite from Sugar Land, Texas, who lost her last baby molar only last month, turned the championships into her personal playground and it appears likely to remain that way -- at least until she reaches maturity.
That may not be as much of a problem for Lipinski as it is for other skaters -- she has already had her growth potential assessed and she might not reach much more than 1.5 metres.

Anyone thinking they will get the jump on Lipinski as the sport turns towards the 1998 Winter Olympics will have to start immediately because she plans only a couple of days off to savour her victory before beginning her preparations for Nagano.
"I'll g to training, start new programmes and get ready for next season," she said, hinting that a quadruple could be added to her already formidable arsenal of jumps.
"I think for next year I have to get faster and improve the presentation. I will jump higher too."

Lipinski replaces Sonia Henie as the youngest women's champion but admitted earlier in the week she did not know much about the legendary Norwegian, her all-consuming interest in skating being directed more to her own time on the ice.

She spends four hours a day, five days a week, practising with her coach Richard Callaghan, whose biggest problem has been keeping his charge from endlessly repeating each jump until she lands it to her satisfaction.
Not only is she dedicated to her sport, she shows great discipline with her studies. After four hours on the ice she spends another four with her private tutors, with impressive results.

However, according to her mother, in every other aspect of her life, she is a remarkably ordinary teenager, one who likes listening to the Smashing Pumpkins pop group, hanging out at the mall with friends and baking cakes.
"I used to worry if all this was too much but right now she seems to have a great balance with her life. She's having so much fun," said Pat Lipinksi.
"She doesn't talk about skating with her friends. They're normal teenagers, the kind who run into the house, up the stairs close the door and turn on the music."
With the Olympics approaching and the United States quickly turning its attention on its pixie gold medal hopeful, that normality may be about to disappear.

Before the skaters had received their medals, a large American media contingent were licking their lips at the prospect of a rivalry which might go some way towards matching the Tonya Harding-Nancy Kerrigan soap opera of 1994.
"It will be a rivalry for the next 25 years," said Kwan, smiling across at Lipinski. "We're both young.
"I don't know how long she's planning to skate but I'll be there -- always."
